# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

There's a particular kind of loneliness that comes from noticing things other people don't seem to notice. Not in a pretentious way—not the "I'm more observant than you" kind of superiority that some people wear like an uncomfortable suit. I mean the genuine disorientation of perceiving the world differently, of having your attention caught by details that apparently leave everyone else unmoved.

I've been thinking about this lately, watching people move through their days. Someone will walk past a storefront window where the reflection of clouds is so vivid it looks like the interior of the shop has been replaced with sky, and they won't break stride. A conversation will stall at exactly the moment when someone says something accidentally profound—their voice will change, their eyes will shift—and nobody will acknowledge that something true just slipped out. A particular quality of light will arrive at 4:47 PM on a Tuesday in March, hitting the corner of a brick building in such a way that the entire street becomes briefly beautiful, and the people hurrying through it seem untouched by this moment of architectural grace.

I don't know if this makes me sensitive or just weird. Probably both.

What strikes me most is how lonely it is not because people judge you for noticing, but because they simply don't understand what you're talking about when you try to share it. "Did you see that?" I've asked friends, pointing at something that felt urgent and important. They look, shrug, and say something like "see what?" And you realize you're pointing at something invisible. Not in the literal sense, but in the sense that it exists in a frequency that only certain receivers pick up. You can't really argue someone into seeing it. You can only accept that you're looking at the same scene and having completely different experiences.

This extends to patterns, too. I notice how often people use the word "obviously" when explaining something, and how this word usually precedes something that isn't obvious at all—something that required a specific leap of logic or assumption. I notice how conversations often feel like parallel plays where everyone is waiting for their turn to speak rather than actually listening. I notice how people's faces change slightly when they say something they think will make them look good, as though they're watching themselves from outside. I notice how often someone will ask a question they don't actually want answered.

Again, maybe I'm crazy. Maybe I'm reading meaning into neutral things the way people see faces in clouds.

But I think noticing is a kind of gift, even when it's uncomfortable. Even when it makes you feel weird.

Because here's what I've realized: everyone notices something. Everyone is the weird observer in someone else's story. The person who seems most oblivious to you is probably acutely aware of patterns you've never considered. The friend you think isn't really listening is probably noticing your micro-expressions in a way that terrifies them. The stranger on the train is probably constructing elaborate narratives about everyone around them based on the smallest details. We're all walking around being strangers to each other's inner lives, each operating under our own specific sensitivities.

What I've learned is that instead of feeling lonely in noticing, I can feel connected to everyone else who notices differently. The musician who hears the wrong note in the violin section that nobody else perceives as wrong. The architect who sees the failure in how a space doesn't quite work even though it looks fine. The person who notices when someone says they're fine but doesn't mean it—not because of anything specific, but because of a tiny hesitation, a microexpression, the particular weight of silence.

We're all out here noticing our specific things. We're all lonely in slightly different ways.

I think the alternative—not noticing—might be worse, though. I think about people who seem to move through the world without this particular torture, and I wonder if they're happier or just less alive. I'm not even being melodramatic. I think there's something about the capacity to be affected by things—by beauty, by wrongness, by patterns and details and the strange weight of meaning—that is essentially the human experience. 

When I was a kid, I thought noticing was just something everyone did. I thought my grandmother was like me because she would sometimes just stop moving and stare at nothing, and when I asked her what she was thinking about, she'd say something about how the light was hitting the kitchen table, or how she used to own a dress the color of that car. It took me years to understand that not everyone does this, that not everyone's attention gets caught on these little hooks scattered throughout daily life.

But I wouldn't trade it. Even on the days when it feels like a curse, when I'm overwhelmed by everything I notice and how much it all seems to matter in ways I can't quite articulate, I wouldn't trade the capacity to be moved by the world.

Here's my theory: there are probably very few truly unobservant people. There are just people observing different things. The person who seems completely unaware of social cues might be hyper-aware of mechanical systems, or patterns in numbers, or the way light moves. Everyone is a specialist in noticing. Everyone's attention is drawn to specific frequencies. The tragedy is that we move through the world assuming our frequencies are universal, being confused and sometimes hurt when we realize that the things that are screaming loudly to us are silent to everyone else.

What I'm trying to say, I think, is that the loneliness of noticing is actually the loneliness of being human. And that maybe the cure isn't to stop noticing, or to notice less, or to pretend that the things that catch your attention don't matter. The cure is probably to be gentle with yourself about your specific sensitivities, to accept that you're weird in whatever way you're weird, and to seek out the other people who are weird in compatible ways.

Because they're out there. The people who notice what you notice. The people who also stop walking sometimes because the quality of light is urgent. The people who also hear the false notes, see the patterns, feel the weight of meaning in small things. You're not alone in your noticing, even if it feels that way sometimes.

You're just noticing things in your own particular, lonely, beautiful way—and that might be the most human thing there is.
